blocks.text: A set is one of the simplest and most powerful ideas in all of mathematics: an unordered collection of distinct objects, with no repeats and no notion of order. From this single idea, and a small handful of operations on it, an enormous amount of mathematics and, closer to home, an enormous amount of everyday AI engineering is built. Vocabularies in a tokenizer, the feature columns available to a model, the unique user IDs in a log file, all of these are sets, and the operations covered in this lesson, union, intersection, difference, and complement, are the operations you reach for constantly when cleaning, filtering, and deduplicating data.

blocks.alt: From a collection of objects to set operations used in AI pipelines
blocks.caption: A set groups distinct elements; operations on sets power dedup and filtering

1. What a Set Is

Formally, a set is an unordered collection of distinct elements. "Unordered" means that the set containing 1, 2, and 3 is exactly the same set as the one containing 3, 1, and 2; there is no first or second element. "Distinct" means that repeating an element does nothing new: writing an element twice does not create a multiset, it just describes the same set again.

Sets are usually named with a capital letter and written with curly braces listing their elements, such as A equals the set containing 1, 2, 3. Membership is written with the symbol for "element of": 2 is an element of A, while 5 is not an element of A. These two symbols, element of and not an element of, are the most basic building blocks of set notation, and everything else in this lesson is built from asking questions about membership.
2. Set Builder Notation

Rather than listing every element, a set is often described by a rule that its elements must satisfy. This is called set builder notation, written as the set of x such that some condition on x holds. For example, the set of x such that x is an even integer between 1 and 10 describes exactly 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, without listing them directly in the definition.

Set builder notation becomes essential once a set is too large, or too irregular, to list by hand, such as the set of all real numbers greater than zero, or the set of all valid usernames matching a particular pattern. It is also the natural way to describe filtered subsets of data: "the set of all users whose session length exceeds five minutes" is a set builder description of a filtering operation.
3. The Empty Set

The empty set is the unique set that contains no elements at all, written with the special symbol that looks like an oslash, or equivalently as an empty pair of braces. It is a perfectly valid set, not an error or an undefined value, and it plays a role similar to zero in arithmetic: it is the starting point that other sets are built up from, and it is the result of intersecting two sets that share nothing in common.

blocks.title: A common trap
blocks.content: The empty set is not the same thing as a set containing the empty set. The set containing the empty set has exactly one element, namely the empty set itself, so its size is 1, not 0.

code.content:
empty = set()
print(len(empty))       # 0
print(empty == set())   # True

wrapped = {frozenset()}
print(len(wrapped))     # 1, a set holding one element (the empty set)

blocks.text: 4. Subsets

A set A is a subset of a set B if every element of A is also an element of B, written A is a subset of B. Every set is automatically a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set, since there are no elements in the empty set that could fail to be in some other set B; the condition is vacuously true.

A proper subset tightens this slightly: A is a proper subset of B if A is a subset of B and A is not equal to B, meaning B must contain at least one element that A does not. The distinction matters when reasoning about strict containment, for example when saying that the set of nouns recognized by a tokenizer is a proper subset of its entire vocabulary, implying the vocabulary is strictly larger.

blocks.text: 5. Union

The union of two sets A and B, written A union B, is the set of all elements that belong to A, to B, or to both. Union combines two collections into one, keeping every distinct element exactly once; nothing from either set is dropped, and duplicates that appear in both sets are still only counted once, since a set never holds repeats.

blocks.alt: Venn diagram of the union of A and B
blocks.caption: The union shades every region belonging to A or B, including the overlap

blocks.text: 6. Intersection

The intersection of two sets A and B, written A intersect B, is the set of elements that belong to both A and B at the same time. Where union asks "is it in either," intersection asks the stricter question "is it in both," so the intersection is always at most as large as either original set.

blocks.alt: Venn diagram of the intersection of A and B
blocks.caption: The intersection shades only the overlapping region shared by A and B

blocks.text: Intersection is the natural mathematical model of "what do these two things have in common," which is precisely the question asked when comparing two users vocabularies, two feature sets, or two tag lists.
7. Difference and Complement

The difference of A and B, written A minus B, is the set of elements that belong to A but not to B. Difference is not symmetric: A minus B generally produces a different result than B minus A, since the first keeps only what is unique to A, while the second keeps only what is unique to B.

blocks.alt: Venn diagram of the difference A minus B
blocks.caption: The difference keeps only the part of A that does not overlap with B

blocks.text: 7.1 The Complement

The complement of a set A, written A with a superscript c, is defined relative to some agreed universal set U that contains everything under discussion; the complement is every element of U that is not in A, equivalently U minus A. Complement only makes sense once a universe has been fixed; there is no such thing as "everything not in A" without first agreeing on the boundary of "everything."
8. Cardinality

The cardinality of a set is simply the number of distinct elements it contains, written as vertical bars around the set name, such as the cardinality of A. For a finite set this is an ordinary count: the cardinality of the set containing 3, 7, and 9 is 3. Cardinality is what makes sets countable and comparable in size, which matters enormously once sets start representing things like vocabularies or datasets with millions of entries.

A useful identity connects the cardinality of a union to the cardinalities of the two original sets and their intersection: the cardinality of A union B equals the cardinality of A, plus the cardinality of B, minus the cardinality of A intersect B. The subtraction corrects for double counting the elements that appear in both sets, which would otherwise be counted twice by naively adding the two sizes.

code.content:
A = {1, 2, 3, 4}
B = {3, 4, 5, 6}
print(len(A))            # 4
print(len(B))             # 4
print(len(A & B))         # 2, the overlap
print(len(A | B))         # 6, not 8, because the overlap is not double counted
assert len(A | B) == len(A) + len(B) - len(A & B)

blocks.text: 9. Sets Versus Other Collections

It helps to be precise about what a set is not. A list or array is ordered and allows repeats, so the list containing 1, 1, 2 is different from the list containing 2, 1, 1, and both are different from the list containing 1, 2. A tuple is similarly ordered. A set collapses both of those distinctions away: order is discarded and repeats are discarded, leaving only "which distinct things are present."

This is exactly why sets are the right tool for deduplication: converting a list into a set automatically removes every repeated value, keeping only one copy of each distinct element, and converting back to a list afterward yields the deduplicated collection.

blocks.text: This distinction has direct performance consequences. Checking whether an element exists in a Python list requires scanning the list from the start, an operation that takes time proportional to the list length in the worst case. Checking membership in a set uses hashing to jump almost directly to the answer, which is why converting a large list to a set before running many membership checks is a standard and important optimization.
10. The Python Set Data Structure

Python provides a built in set type that mirrors the mathematical definition closely: unordered, no duplicates, and backed by a hash table, which is why membership testing with the "in" operator runs in roughly constant time rather than scanning the whole collection the way a list membership check does. This is one of the most practically important facts about sets for anyone writing data pipelines: swapping a list for a set can turn an accidentally quadratic deduplication or lookup routine into a linear one.
10.1 Core Operations in Python

items: add(x) inserts a single element x into the set, doing nothing if x is already present.
remove(x) deletes x from the set, raising an error if x is not present; discard(x) does the same but stays silent if x is missing.
union, intersection, difference, and their operators (pipe, ampersand, minus) implement the four operations covered above.
issubset and issuperset check the subset relationship in either direction.
A set comprehension, such as {x * x for x in range(5)}, builds a set directly from set builder style notation.

blocks.text: 10.2 Frozen Sets

Python also provides frozenset, an immutable version of a set that cannot be modified after creation. Because ordinary sets are mutable, they cannot themselves be placed inside another set or used as a dictionary key; frozenset solves this by offering a hashable, read only set that can be nested, which is exactly why the earlier example wrapping the empty set used frozenset rather than set.

code.content:
immutable_tags = frozenset({"python", "ml"})
# immutable_tags.add("nlp")  # would raise AttributeError

nested = {frozenset({1, 2}), frozenset({3, 4})}
print(nested)

blocks.text: 11. AI Relevance: Vocabulary Sets in NLP

Every tokenizer used in natural language processing is built around a vocabulary, and a vocabulary is fundamentally a set: a fixed collection of distinct tokens, where each token either belongs to the vocabulary or does not, with no notion of order and no meaning attached to repeats. Building a vocabulary from a training corpus is literally a union operation applied across every document: take the set of unique tokens appearing in each document, then union all of those sets together.

Out of vocabulary handling is a direct application of set difference: given a new sentence, the tokens not present in the trained vocabulary are exactly the set difference between the tokens in the sentence and the vocabulary set, and these are the tokens that must be mapped to a special unknown token or broken down further by a subword tokenizer.

code.content:
corpus = ["the cat sat", "the dog ran", "cats and dogs"]
vocabulary = set()
for sentence in corpus:
    vocabulary |= set(sentence.lower().split())
print(sorted(vocabulary))
# ['and', 'cat', 'cats', 'dog', 'dogs', 'ran', 'sat', 'the']

new_sentence_tokens = set("the fox jumped".split())
out_of_vocabulary = new_sentence_tokens - vocabulary
print(out_of_vocabulary)   # {'fox', 'jumped'}

blocks.text: This same union-based construction scales directly to how large language model tokenizers are built: byte pair encoding and similar subword algorithms start from a base vocabulary set of individual characters or bytes, then iteratively grow that set by merging the most frequent adjacent pairs, at every step still maintaining a strict set of distinct tokens with no duplicates.
12. AI Relevance: Feature Sets and Deduplication Pipelines

When comparing two versions of a machine learning model, engineers frequently ask questions that are pure set operations on feature names: which features are shared by both models (intersection), which features were added in the new version (difference), and which features exist in either version (union). Reasoning about model changes this way keeps the comparison precise and avoids manually eyeballing long feature lists.

Deduplication pipelines, whether removing duplicate rows from a training dataset, duplicate user records from a database, or duplicate documents from a retrieval index, all reduce to the same underlying operation: converting a collection with possible repeats into a set, which discards the repeats by definition, then converting back to whatever ordered structure the downstream code expects.

blocks.text: 13. Worked Example

Two recommendation systems log the set of product IDs they each recommended to a user in one session. System A recommended products 101, 102, 103, 104. System B recommended products 103, 104, 105, 106. Find the products recommended by either system, the products recommended by both, the products unique to System A, and the total number of distinct products recommended across both systems.

The check via cardinality confirms the result: the cardinality of A is 4, the cardinality of B is 4, and the cardinality of their intersection is 2, so the cardinality of their union is 4 plus 4 minus 2, which equals 6, matching the direct count above.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Treating a set as ordered, and relying on the order elements were inserted in; Python sets make no such guarantee and iteration order should never be depended on.
Confusing the empty set with a set containing the empty set, or with zero; they are different objects with different cardinalities.
Assuming set difference is symmetric; A minus B and B minus A are generally different sets unless A and B are disjoint or identical.
Forgetting that complement requires a fixed universal set U; asking for "the complement of A" without specifying U is not well defined.
Double counting shared elements when computing the size of a union by hand, instead of subtracting the intersection size once.

Key Takeaway

A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements, and the four core operations, union, intersection, difference, and complement, give a precise vocabulary for combining, comparing, and filtering collections. These are not abstract exercises: they are the exact operations running underneath vocabulary construction in NLP, feature comparisons between model versions, and deduplication in any data pipeline.

The next two lessons build directly on this foundation. Relations describe structured connections between the elements of two sets, and functions add the further constraint that each input connects to exactly one output, a constraint that turns out to be the mathematical backbone of every neural network.
